title: What the textiles in a central bank’s working rooms can tell us
summary: Alberto Ríos uses the launch of Banco de España’s textile catalogue to ask why objects familiar to generations of employees remained so poorly understood as a collection. Carpets, tapestries and ceremonial hangings were acquired for particular rooms and purposes. Seeing them in place every day made them part of the institution’s routine, but could obscure their artistic interest and history. In his opening address, the director general argues that treating an object, its room and the people who used it as related evidence allows researchers to recover more of that history.

This is the latest stage in an established programme. The bank’s three-volume 2020 catalogue studied more than 1,400 works of painting, sculpture, drawing and photography by approximately 500 artists. A separate 2023 study examined its clocks. Ríos presents the textile project as a way of bringing the same attention to objects that performed practical as well as representational work. A carpet could make a room more comfortable while helping mark its status. A hanging could alter how a space felt and how it functioned. Working backwards from the surviving piece to its commission and intended location changes what can be said about the building and the institution that occupied it.

Ríos distinguishes the roles of the people who would speak after him. Antonio Sama led much of the research into the historical pieces. Curator Yolanda Romero would explain the project’s development and the entry of contemporary textiles into the collection. Patricia Esquivias was to discuss her recently acquired work, La fiesta de la Trashumancia. Those are introductions, not a transcript of the speakers’ findings. Their juxtaposition illustrates the director’s point that contemporary artists can put inherited materials and techniques to different uses.

The catalogue and the accompanying exhibition also serve different readers. A visitor can encounter an object’s scale and surface directly. The published descriptions, photographs and provenance research remain available after the exhibition closes. Ríos credits the bank’s heritage division and the researchers, photographers and editorial team for that work. The address concerns stewardship and access to cultural collections. It supplies no appraisal values, acquisition budget or evidence on the central bank’s monetary or investment policy.

questions.question: Which objects have contemporary records linking them to a particular institutional use?
questions.detail: Ríos explains why location and function matter without identifying the archival proof for each object. Examine catalogue entries beside room plans, commission records, inventories and dated photographs to distinguish a documented use from a later curatorial inference. This changes how confidently a historian can reconstruct the bank’s working environment.

questions.question: How do the contemporary acquisitions relate to the older collection?
questions.detail: The address introduces Esquivias and Romero but does not reproduce their accounts. Consult the artist’s statement, the curator’s catalogue essay and the object’s accession record to determine whether the connection lies in material, technique, subject matter or curatorial selection. Those alternatives carry different implications for interpreting the institution’s collecting policy.

questions.question: Which information is preserved beyond the temporary exhibition?
questions.detail: Ríos assigns that role to the catalogue. Compare its object records, photography and references with the exhibition guide and accessible digital holdings. A researcher who needs to establish provenance or trace an object between rooms will require different evidence from a visitor interested mainly in seeing the work.

limitation: The original is the director’s opening address. The curatorial and artist presentations it introduces are not transcribed in the speech.
